Azerbaijan is the undisputed global capital of mud volcanoes, housing nearly 400 of the world's estimated 1,000 formations. Unlike magmatic volcanoes that spew molten lava, these features erupt a thick, mineral-rich slurry of mud and water driven by high-pressure gas pockets deep underground. Primarily located along the Caspian coast, they range from tiny "puddles" to massive mounds nearly 400 meters high. This phenomenon occurs when tectonic movement forces gas and solids through the earth's crust, often signaling the presence of massive oil and gas reserves. The resulting landscape is an eerie, grey, moon-like terrain that is both scientifically vital and a major tourist draw
NASA Research: Scientists from NASA have used these volcanoes as a "terrestrial analog" to study similar structures on Mars, hoping to find clues about the Red Planet's subsurface.

15. Most divided cities on earth are divided by walls, rivers, or ceasefire lines. This one is divided by all the usual markers — but for a few months every winter, it acquires an additional and entirely modern layer of division: it splits into two different time zones. The city has been partitioned since the 1970s following a military intervention, with the northern sector administered separately from the southern. Both halves observe the same time for most of the year — but when clocks are adjusted for daylight saving, one side moves and the other does not, leaving a one-hour gap between neighbours who can see each other across a UN buffer zone. It holds the distinction of being the only capital city of its kind anywhere on earth.
